sources.headline: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
sources.text: Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history. It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government. Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy. Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe. Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

sources.headline: Israeli Jews Across the Spectrum Face an Election of Fears
sources.text: Supporters and opponents of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have expressed intense anxieties about isolation abroad, security at home and the future of Israel’s identity.

Opponents accuse Netanyahu of stoking tensions with Iran before Israel's election

Issued on: 26/10/2026 - 18:11

Israel's defence minister denied on Monday (October 26) reports of a rift between PM Netanyahu and the army over Iran, before the vote.  Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" in the US-Israeli war on Iran. His main rival, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has accused him of playing up the Iran threat when it suits him politically, and of failing to accomplish his war goals. FRANCE 24's Kethevane Gorjestani tells us more.

sources.headline: 'Yes Bibi or No Bibi': Netanyahu's political future overshadows Israel's election
sources.text:
Published on
26 October 2026 - 15:23 GMT+1
As Israelis prepare to vote in Tuesday's parliamentary election, questions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future remain central to the campaign, alongside national security, accountability for the 7 October 2023 attacks and the consequences of three years of war.
Former Israeli government spokesperson Eylon Levy told Euronews that the debate over whether Netanyahu should remain prime minister has become the defining fault line in Israeli politics, making cooperation between parties increasingly difficult.
"The question of whether he should or shouldn't be prime minister has contaminated, frozen, poisoned Israeli politics for a decade now," Levy said.
"Like him or loathe him, he really is a once-in-a-century kind of leader," he added.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces questions over the responsibility for the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, while his ongoing criminal trial remains another source of political division.
Levy suggested that Netanyahu's eventual departure could fundamentally reshape the country's political landscape.
"The day after Netanyahu, whenever that happens, I think we can expect to see Israeli politics being realigned. Until then, the battle lines really are drawn around, yes Bibi or no Bibi," he said.
An election in the shadow of 7 October
The vote, Israel's first since the 2023 attacks, comes amid demands for a state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed Hamas to carry out the assault.
"These elections are taking place in the shadow of the October 7 massacre and that issue is absolutely everywhere," Levy told Euronews.
He identified three central issues: responsibility for the attacks, Hamas's continued rule in Gaza and the social and economic costs of the war.
According to Levy, the unresolved question of Hamas's future has fuelled public anger, with political parties competing over who can deliver lasting security for Israel.
Prospect of renewed war with Iran
Beyond domestic issues, Levy predicted that military hostilities with Iran could resume after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
"I think that a return to war in Iran is extremely likely after the midterm elections," he said.
Levy described the current standoff with Tehran as unsustainable, pointing to tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian military activity in the region.
He also suggested that US President Donald Trump was reluctant to resume hostilities before the midterms because of concerns about oil prices.
"President Trump has said he doesn't want to return to the war before the midterms, clearly worrying what will happen to oil prices," Levy said.
According to Levy, Netanyahu would be likely to seek a more decisive outcome from any future confrontation, including the removal of Iran's leadership.
Yet for Levy, the prospect of change extends beyond Israel's regional security policies. He argued that Netanyahu's eventual departure could allow political parties to cooperate across divisions that have shaped Israeli politics for years.

sources.headline: This center-right former general could unseat Netanyahu as Prime Minister in Israel
sources.text:
A former Israeli general is the main center-right challenger hoping to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israeli elections this week.
Transcript
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: Benjamin Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister - more than 19 years if you add up all the terms he's served. This week, he's battling to stay in power. On Tuesday, Israelis go to the polls after years of wars across the region. NPR's Daniel Estrin is in Israel and has this story on the former general trying to unseat Netanyahu and his far-right government.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: No. 1, Gadi Eisenkot, yeah.DANIEL ESTRIN, BYLINE: Gadi Eisenkot is Netanyahu's leading opponent. At a stump speech a few weeks ago, I watch him take the stage. He's a short man with cropped white hair, wearing all black.GADI EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: The event is in Kiryat Gat, a city near the Gaza border. Historically, it's a conservative Netanyahu stronghold. This crowd knows Eisenkot as the former military chief of staff appointed by Netanyahu a decade ago. He came back into the public spotlight days after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023. He joined Netanyahu's war Cabinet. Very soon, the nation saw Eisenkot crying over his son's casket.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).UNIDENTIFIED PEOPLE: (Crying).ESTRIN: His son was a soldier killed in Gaza. The very next day, his nephew was killed fighting in Gaza. Eisenkot tells this crowd that after the first three months of war, he thought things were going in the wrong direction.EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: "I saw a deep dysfunction in the decision-making process," he says. "I saw that political and personal considerations were put above everything else." He means Netanyahu. He's pledging to voters the first thing he'll do as prime minister is to do the thing Netanyahu has refused to do, to launch an official national investigation into the security failure of October 7.EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: In the crowd, I met Yair Amar. He told me he always used to vote for "Bibi" - Benjamin Netanyahu.YAIR AMAR: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: But he says Netanyahu is responsible for all the Israelis killed on October 7. And Eisenkot?AMAR: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: He says, "he's straight" - like a straight shooter, down to earth. He's everything Netanyahu isn't, says Amos Harel, an Israeli defense analyst for the newspaper Haaretz.AMOS HAREL: Many Israelis wish for a saner future, for somebody who perhaps is not as charismatic and doesn't look the part of an American senator but is one of us and is seen as somebody who sacrificed a lot.ESTRIN: The race is very, very tight. Most polls show Eisenkot's camp ahead of Netanyahu's camp. But those same polls show that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to victory. The election could tip based on a small amount of votes, or it could end in a stalemate and force a repeat election next spring. If that were to happen, Netanyahu would stay in power without a new mandate from the public but with full authority to make fateful decisions like going to war. If Eisenkot wins, he has promised to crack down on settler expansion and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. He talks about reaching diplomatic agreements in all the wars Netanyahu has kept open. But there's one thing he's made clear. He would not withdraw troops from Lebanon and Gaza anytime soon.EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: "Truth be told," Eisenkot told the crowd, "it will take a lot of time." He said the Israeli military presence in both places is necessary until Hamas and Hezbollah's military forces are dismantled. And on the biggest question of all, how to solve Israel's conflict with the Palestinians...EISENKOT: (Non-English language spoken).ESTRIN: ...Eisenkot boasted to the crowd that he never said the solution was two states for two peoples, meaning creating a Palestinian state alongside Israel. That is the vision that the U.S. and the majority of the world has advocated for decades. Eisenkot thinks Israel should preserve possibilities for a solution in the future. After October 7, Israelis do not want to discuss a Palestinian state. Analyst Amos Harel.HAREL: It's not something that the Israeli public can swallow at this time. More and more people suspect that the Arabs, the Palestinians are out to kill us and that the world is out to get us.ESTRIN: That mistrust of Arabs has a direct impact on Eisenkot's chances in the race. Polls suggest the opposition parties would easily win if they'd be willing to share power with Arab political parties representing Israel's Arab citizens. But opposition parties say they won't partner with Arab parties, which is a victory for Netanyahu. He's running a campaign claiming the Arab political parties pose a threat, says Harel.HAREL: The fact that, in spite of his political weakness, Netanyahu managed to reach a sort of a consensus among the Israeli public that the Arab parties, led by Arab Israeli citizens, are illegitimate as partners is quite amazing.ESTRIN: This is not a race of conservatives versus liberals, right versus left. Eisenkot is leading a group of politicians who are largely right wing - not the far right of Netanyahu's camp, but right wing, focused on boosting Israel's military for whatever dangers are to come and recruiting religious ultra-Orthodox Jews to the military, trying to tell Israelis, it's OK not to vote for Netanyahu. I'll make sure Israel stays strong.ANAT BEN-ARI: I'm trusting him on the military level, but is it enough?ESTRIN: High school theater teacher Anat Ben-Ari came to hear Eisenkot speak, and she's almost nervous voicing an unpopular opinion out loud. She thinks he shouldn't shy away from peace agreements.BEN-ARI: The only way to end war, all the history says that, is by agreements - people talking to people, even enemies, mostly enemies. And I think we should also pay the price for peace in order for less people to die here and not always live on our swords.ESTRIN: With days to go before elections, war is fresh on Israelis' minds. Netanyahu is campaigning for votes with a new promise. If he wins, he'll partner with the U.S. to launch a new attack on Iran. Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Kiryat Gat in southern Israel.

sources.headline: These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate in Israel's election
sources.text:
By
Dov Lieber
Senior Reporter
Dov Lieber is a senior reporter for CBS News based in Tel Aviv, covering political, diplomatic and security developments across Israel, the Palestinian Territories and the broader Middle East.
Read Full Bio
Updated on: October 26, 2026 / 12:54 PM EDT
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents.Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent. Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over. "It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute.This will be the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday with their country still fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third. Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes.The Netanyahu campNetanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.
He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started. President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.
A campaign billboard depicting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump is seen in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 26, 2026.
JACK GUEZ/AFP/Getty Images
Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat.
Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb." Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel.Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader."Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him.""He's the king of Israel," Abraham added. The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc"Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power. The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.
Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Tel Aviv, Israel.
Erik Marmor/picture alliance/Getty Images
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu. Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv.""This time, it won't work for him," he said. Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas — something Netanyahu has thus far blocked.Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu. "Eisenkot is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said.
The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side.One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side. Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population."The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute. More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News."The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future." There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales — in either direction — toward a new coalition government.
Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service.
Ultra-Orthodox Jewish leaders of the Breslev Hasidic community take part in a rally against mandatory military conscription on Oct. 12, 2026, in Netanya, Israel.
Amir Levy/Getty Images
It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners. Not all election outcomes are neat and tidyIn the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government. One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on. Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. sources.headline: Israel election: What happens after polls close?
sources.text: JERUSALEM — Israel holds a parliamentary election on Oct 27, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.When will we know who won?It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.Voting starts at 7am (1pm, Singapore time) and ends at 10pm, when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.A clear picture may emerge quickly but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.The final tally is expected by Oct 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov 4.Why is it so complicated?Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be ​held every four years but early elections have been frequent.The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.What happens after the results are published?After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition ​of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government. REUTERS

sources.headline: ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election
sources.text: As Israel prepares to go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people.Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign.Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention.“We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.”Gadi Eisenkot championed the “Dahiya doctrine” in the 2006 war with Hezbollah, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APNeither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan.Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the “Dahiya doctrine”, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes.“Eisenkot talks of defeating Hamas, while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.”Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a 48-second election video showing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.”The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.”The chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians in Gaza, pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change.“I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning.“For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.”In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied by the struggle to find food and water to follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials.Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis.Candidates in the upcoming Israeli election include Yair Golan of the Democrats party (left billboard) and the Arab-led Joint List. Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersYet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future.They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future.“A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.”Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turned hunger into a weapon of war. And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed since 7 October 2023.“I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City.“Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change. As I see it, their goal is to destroy Gaza and the foundations of life here.”

sources.headline: Gadi Eisenkot campaigns on Moroccan roots in challenge to Netanyahu
sources.text:
Ahead of Tuesday's elections, party advertisements greet people arriving by train to the outskirts of the western Israeli city of Sderot.
Campaign posters with various slogans promote the right-wing Likud and the far-right Otzma Yehudit parties. However, one poster is seen more than any others: that of the liberal Yashar party.
Its slogan, "Rosh Memshala Dialna," combines the terms "prime minister" in Hebrew and the words "of our own" in Moroccan Arabic.
And there is a good reason why Eisenkot's campaign in Sderot and other cities on Israel's sociopolitical periphery focuses on his Moroccan roots.
Eisenkot's Mizrahi background
Sderot — located in the Negev desert, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) to Tel Aviv's south and just a kilometer away from the Gaza border — is a city with a large Moroccan Jewish community. In recent decades, the city has become symbolic of Moroccan-Jewish culture in Israel, finding its expression in music, cinema and state politics. Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Historically, Sderot is considered a bastion of the Israeli right, and especially a stronghold of Prime MinisterBenjamin Netanyahu's Likud. In 2022, Likud received more than 40% of the votes in Sderot, compared with 23% nationwide. Other members of Israel's far-right coalition received a lot of support there in the last election.
This pattern reflects deeper historical divisions in Israel between Ashkenazim, or Jews of European origin, and Mizrahim, or Jews mostly from Middle Eastern and North African backgrounds. According to estimates, half of Israel's Jewish population is of Mizrahi origin, amounting to about 4 million people.
Mizrahi Jews have faced discrimination and neglect since the early days of the Israeli state. This inequality still shapes the economic and social reality in Israel ― and its political discourse.
The issue has received special attention in the 2026 campaign. Eisenkot, Netanyahu's major challenger, is of Moroccan origin and grew up in Eilat, a city with a large North African Jewish population. Eisenkot's Yashar party accused Likud of sidelining its Mizrahi politicians. The campaign slogan, "Netanyahu: Let the Mizrahim give interviews,” mocked that omission. A sticker campaign in Sderot called for a Mizrahi prime ministerImage: Felix Tamsut/DW
On live television, the right-wing journalist Yinon Magal — one of Netanyahu's most vocal supporters — claimed that Eisenkot was being controlled by elitist Ashkenazim and called him a "monkey."
Netanyahu, who is of European origin, condemned the remark.
Morocco-born Daniel Ben-Simon, an award-winning Israeli journalist and a former member of parliament, told DW that Eisenkot's embrace of his roots might have been forced upon him by Magal's comments — but it has historical value nevertheless.
"People don't use terms like 'Dialna' with pride," Ben-Simon said, referring to Eisenkot's embrace of the Arabic term "of our own" in campaign posters. He said Israeli society had long tried to erase the Arab identities of North African Jews.
Eisenkot's embrace of his identity serves as a way of "leaving the frame" set by society. "By using such a term, you're creating a new identity: an Israeli-Moroccan identity," Ben-Simon said. "Eisenkot is the first to allow this double identity to be expressed and still feel at home."
Israel's historical divide
After Israel's founding, the ruling socialist party, Mapai, whose leadership was largely Ashkenazi, pursued discriminatory policies against Mizrahim. Mizrahim were often expected to "Europeanize” rather than preserve their own culture, heritage, or Arabic language. Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
These inequalities also took a material form. In the state's early decades, while European immigrants often received better housing and jobs, many Jews from Arab-speaking countries were sent to Ma'abarot, or temporary transit camps, often in remote areas with little infrastructure. Many later became "development towns,” which remained underfunded compared with Israel's central regions. That in turn resulted in poverty. Sderot, in the south, is one of the best-known development towns.
For many Mizrahim, limited access to jobs, education and infrastructure symbolized long-standing exclusion by the Mapai establishment. Likud, founded as a right-wing alliance in 1973, used this frustration effectively under Menachem Begin. Mizrahi support for Begin helped produce the Mahapach, or upheaval, when Likud first defeated the socialist camp and took power. Since then, Mizrahim have often been associated with Likud, even though the party has never had a Mizrahi leader.Sderot's changing demographics
Over the past two decades, Sderot's proximity to Gaza has made the city a frequent target of rocket attacks launched by the militant group Hamas. During the Hamas-led terrorist attacks on October 7, 2023, the city of Sderot was hit especially hard. More than 50 people were killed. In the three years since the attack, the city's population has grown by about 5,000 people, bringing it to 40,000, with many young families making the town their home, both as a result of idealism and government benefits.The Sderot memorial for the victims of October 7Image: Felix Tamsut/DW
Walking around the town, it's hard not to notice that the so-called national-religious community is becoming increasingly dominant. This community tends to vote for Bezalel Smotrich's far-right Religious Zionism party, a main member of Netanyahu's coalition. Though votes for Smotrich and his party are de facto votes for Netanyahu's bloc, the prime minister's Likud party itself could suffer losses in Sderot.
Regardless of the election's results, the perception of Sderot as a city of Moroccan Jews is not bound to change anytime soon. Ben-Simon said Eisenkot's election could serve as an opportunity for reshaping Moroccan Jews' future identity in Israel.
"The connection cities like Sderot have to their Moroccan roots would grow stronger as a result of an Eisenkot win," Ben-Simon said.
Edited by: Shani Rozanes

Agence France-Presse
Published: 1:29am, 26 Oct 2026Updated: 1:29pm, 26 Oct 2026

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday’s Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts.

The remarks came as Israel’s Channel 12 reported, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the prime minister denied.

Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he launched against Iran in February alongside the United States and suggesting that he alone can see it through.
